analysis.title: "More Oil Is Leaving The Gulf Than Before The War": And Here Comes The Shocking Freight Bill
key_insights: Kpler puts Middle East crude and condensate flows at 24.6 million b/d in the week through Oct 18, a conflict high and above Kpler's prewar baseline of 24.4 million b/d (week ending Feb 22). WSJ cites more than 24 million b/d. This comes despite the complete loss of Iran's exports (close to 2 million b/d in February) under the US blockade.

Hormuz transits themselves are still only about 82% of prewar volumes per the WSJ. Kpler's total also counts net ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman and exports from Red Sea ports and UAE/Omani terminals on the Gulf of Oman, so part of the Gulf barrels never transit the strait.

Flow data is disputed. Vortexa puts the same week at 18 million b/d, below the prewar 18.5 million b/d that both firms agree on (narrower crude definitions). For October month to date, Kpler has 16.7 million b/d and Vortexa 15.4 million b/d, both below prewar. Tankers run with AIS off and shipments often appear later as upward revisions.

Flows are lumpy because tankers move in convoys. Satellite images of the biggest Saudi Gulf terminal showed five VLCCs loading on Oct 12-13 and one by Oct 20. LSEG warned Iran is targeting tankers beyond the strait in the Gulf of Oman, which threatens loadings and ship-to-ship transfers.

Attacks on shipping are rising. UKMTO reports 32 attacks around the Arabian peninsula so far in October versus 16 in all of September. The IMO counts 116 attacks and 24 deaths since the war began Feb 28. Kpler counted at least 18 vessel attacks in the past two weeks.

Supply workarounds: Saudi Arabia raised production by a third in September to over 8 million b/d and ships from both Gulf and Red Sea coasts. Iraq is pushing more volume through Hormuz and the UAE (per IEA) has record production. UAE, Saudi and Kuwait hand off crude to buyers' ships outside the strait.

Goldman's new global freight index (weighted average of 25 Platts routes covering 82% of seaborne crude exports) shows the average crude freight rate above $20/bbl versus $3/bbl a year ago. Middle East routes are above $35/bbl and refined products are around $15/bbl.
Long-haul routes are hit hardest. West Africa to Far East Asia freight is up more than $40/bbl y/y, and US Gulf Coast to China and North Sea to Singapore are each up around $35/bbl.

Goldman splits the $20/bbl freight rise into five drivers: Hormuz war risk premium $7, ship-to-ship transfers $4, maritime fuel $4, inefficient tanker allocation and redirections $3, and the Iranian fleet blockade $2. The Hormuz premium and STS transfers together are more than half.
Goldman measures the Hormuz premium as Murban loaded at Fujairah over Basrah loaded in Iraq, up $35/bbl y/y and recently above $40. About 1/6 of global seaborne crude still goes via Hormuz.

Goldman says a recovery in Persian Gulf exports can ease crude prices but lifts freight rates when ship-to-ship transfers drive the export increase. The average Gulf of Oman VLCC round trip for STS has stretched to 23 days versus 10 days for a direct Hormuz run.

VLCC rates on Middle East Gulf to India are about $828,000 a day and to China $765,000 a day (Bloomberg), down from a peak above $1.1 million but more than ten times most of 2024. At about $800K a day, a 2-million-barrel VLCC costs roughly 40 cents/bbl per day, so 13 extra STS days add about $5/bbl.

Benchmarks are priced FOB, so the freight bill shows up in differentials and refining margins. Middle Eastern producers sell nearly half their crude on long-haul routes and are discounting sharply, especially inside-Gulf grades (Basrah, Upper Zakum, Al Shaheen). The Brent-WTI spread widened to $14/bbl last week versus a usual $5, and Canadian, Colombian and Ecuadorian heavy grades are down roughly $10/bbl.

Winners are producers closest to customers, such as Brent in Northwest Europe and Russia's ESPO. Asian refiners are most exposed: China imports 50% of crude via long-haul routes and the rest of Asia 80%.

Goldman says gross refining margins remain very high but net margins after freight, energy and operating costs are already falling. European refiners have cut runs over the past two weeks, and Asian margins are likely approaching levels where further freight increases would be difficult to absorb. EIA reported distillate stocks at seasonal record lows.

Brent rose more than $2 to $110.85 on Wednesday after Iran's President Pezeshkian said the US could not expect dialogue while blockading Iran, near five-month highs. Goldman still forecasts Brent at $90 by year-end and an $80 average in 2027, but says higher freight for longer is upside risk to that forecast.

The author argues freight will stay higher for longer and that Goldman's $90 year-end Brent looks optimistic. The supply shock has moved from the FOB price into shipping, differentials and refining margins.

sector_views.rationale: Tanker rates are near records and Goldman expects the five freight drivers to persist while the conflict continues. The article notes tanker owners get paid either way.

Net margins after freight are falling and Asian margins are near levels where further freight increases would be hard to absorb. Asian refiners import 50% (China) to 80% (rest of Asia) of crude via long-haul routes.

risk_factors: More intense shipping attacks, particularly in the Gulf of Oman where ship-to-ship transfers happen, could cut flows that now look resilient.
Damage to oil infrastructure and a stickier geopolitical risk premium (Goldman).
Freight staying high for longer is upside risk to Goldman's $90 year-end Brent forecast.
Asian refiner net margins are approaching levels where more freight cost is hard to absorb, which could force run cuts and tighten refined product supply.
Distillate stocks at seasonal record lows (EIA) in a market already short on diesel.

charts_described: Goldman chart: Hormuz premium (Murban minus Basrah) plotted against Gulf-to-China freight. The text says the spread is up $35/bbl y/y and recently topped $40.
Bloomberg chart: VLCC rates on Middle East Gulf-to-India and Gulf-to-China routes, down from a peak above $1.1 million a day to $828,000 and $765,000, more than ten times most of 2024.
geopolitical: Iran is stepping up attacks on merchant shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman. UKMTO counts 32 attacks in October versus 16 in September.
The US blockade of Iran has removed Iranian exports of close to 2 million b/d and, per Goldman, appears unlikely to be lifted without a peace deal.
Iran's President Pezeshkian said the US could not expect dialogue while blockading and threatening Iran.
Abu Dhabi is investing tens of billions in a 'Zero Hormuz' bypass, and Fujairah is cited as a strait bypass terminal.
The war began on Feb 28. The IMO counts 116 attacks and 24 deaths since then, and at least one container ship has been sunk in October.
cross_bank_references: Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley (Martijn Rats) are both cited on the same Hormuz flow situation. Rats says oil flow through the strait has remained 'relatively resilient' despite sharply increased attacks.
Kpler and Vortexa disagree on October flows: 16.7 million b/d versus 15.4 million b/d.

tension_points.bull_case: Kpler shows Middle East flows at 24.6 million b/d, above prewar, with Saudi, Iraqi and UAE output higher and bypass routes carrying the recovery. Morgan Stanley's Rats calls flows through the strait relatively resilient.
tension_points.bear_case: Vortexa shows 18 million b/d for the same week and both trackers have October month to date below prewar. Hormuz transits are 82% of prewar, flows are lumpy, and Iran is now attacking tankers in the Gulf of Oman where ship-to-ship transfers occur.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Iranian attacks on tankers and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman that disrupt loadings, which LSEG says is already under way.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman sees Brent falling to $90 by year-end and averaging $80 in 2027 as Gulf exports recover.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman itself says freight is unlikely to fall sharply while the conflict persists and is upside risk to its Brent forecast. The author thinks $90 looks optimistic.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A forecast of $90 requires continuing ship-to-ship transfers without reliable freedom of navigation through the strait, and a US blockade that appears unlikely to be lifted without a peace deal.

theme_stances.key_argument: The five drivers behind higher crude freight rates should persist largely as long as the Middle Eastern conflict remains in its current state.
theme_stances.evidence: freight rates remain seven times higher than a year ago

theme_stances.key_argument: Gulf export volumes have recovered through ship-to-ship transfers and bypass routes, but trackers disagree and flows are lumpy.
theme_stances.evidence: nobody really knows how much oil is leaving the region
